claims.text: A machine-learning predictive approach can integrate lattice-distortion and atomic-disorder descriptors for high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach will predict low phonon thermal conductivity more accurately than existing empirical models.
Lattice distortion is directly linked to phonon-scattering mechanisms in high-entropy alloys.
Atomic disorder is directly linked to phonon-scattering mechanisms in high-entropy alloys.
The target high-entropy alloys are homogeneous solid solutions.
The constituent elements in the target alloys are randomly distributed.
The proposed model will use microstructural data from high-resolution imaging and compositional analysis.
The proposed model will use computational phonon-dispersion calculations to estimate thermal transport.
Laser flash analysis can provide the experimental thermal-transport measurement needed for model validation.
Lattice distortions increase phonon-scattering rates.
Local atomic disorder increases phonon-scattering rates.
Increased phonon scattering caused by intrinsic lattice disorder reduces thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
Variations in the selected microstructural parameters quantitatively correlate with enhanced phonon scattering.
The proposed model will reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error by more than 20% relative to baseline empirical methods on homogeneous high-entropy alloys.
Current empirical or semi-empirical baseline models rely primarily on averaged compositional parameters and omit detailed microstructural inputs.
The proposed approach is applicable only to homogeneous solid-solution high-entropy alloys.
Element segregation, local phase ordering, and other deviations from random elemental distributions may diminish prediction accuracy.
Direct experimental validations linking the proposed microstructural metrics to phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys have not yet been reported.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% reduction in prediction error on a statistically significant homogeneous-sample set would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of statistically significant correlation between the microstructural features and thermal conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.
